Abstract
Emergent intelligence have played a major role in the modern AI development,
manifesting as previously unobserved capabilities enabled by scaling model parame-
ters. While existing studies primarily rely on empirical observations to characterize
this phenomenon, a rigorous theoretical framework remains underexplored. This
study attempts to develop a mathematical approach to formalize emergent intelli-
gence from the perspective of limit theory. Specifically, we introduce a performance
function E(N, P, K), dependent on data size N, model size P and training steps
K, to quantify intelligence behavior. We posit that intelligence emerges as a
transition from finite to effectively infinite knowledge, and thus recast emergent
intelligence as the existence of the limit limN,P,K→∞E(N, P, K), with emer-
gent abilities corresponding to the limiting behavior. Moreover, we show that the
scaling laws of foundation models are approximately governed by the convergence
rate of E(N, P, K) to its asymptotic value E(∞, ∞, ∞). This limit theory helps
reveal that emergent intelligence originates from the existence of a parameter-limit
architecture (referred to as the limit architecture), and that emergent intelligence
rationally corresponds to the learning behavior of this limit system.
By introducing tools from nonlinear Lipschitz operator theory, including charac-
teristic constant Lip(T ) of Lipschitz operator, theory of Lipschitz dual operator
and spectral theory of compact operators, we prove that the necessary and suf-
ficient conditions for existence of the limit architecture is (1) Lip(Ti) ≤1 for
all i > K, for some constant K; (2) there exists a projection operator T such
that ∥Ti −T ∥= ϵi, where P∞

1 Introduction
Foundation models [4] have revolutionized the AI community across a wide range
of domains, including natural language processing [5–9], computer vision [10–13],
multimodal learning [8, 14–17], graph learning [18, 19], and programming languages [20].
These models demonstrate remarkable capabilities in understanding human instructions,
exhibiting knowledge and logical reasoning, and even aligning with human values,
thereby paving a promising path toward general artificial intelligence [21]. The crux
behind these successes lies the phenomenon of ermergent intelligence in foundation
models [22–24]. The concept of emergence has its origins in physics and biology [25–27].
A central insight is captured by the principle of “More Is Different” articulated by
Nobel laureate Philip Anderson [25]. This idea suggests that “quantitative changes in
a system can lead to qualitative changes in behavior” adapted from [28].
Recently, Wei et al. [22] provided a clear definition of emergent ability in large
language models (LLMs) as: “abilities that are not present in smaller-scale models but
are present in large-scale models; thus they cannot be predicted by simply extrapolating
the performance improvements on smaller-scale models”. Such emergent abilities were
first discovered in the GPT-3 family [5], and further motivate the costly effort to train
ever larger models on ever larger datasets, in the hope of unlocking new capabilities.
It is now widely recognized that scaling up foundation models (e.g., data size, model
size, and training steps) can consistently lead to improved performance and sample
efficiency across a wide range of downstream tasks. Empirically, the generalization loss
of foundation models has been observed to follow a predictable power-law relationship
with respect to data size, model size and training steps, a property commonly referred
to as the neural scaling law [29]. In practice, to reduce the cost of discovering effective
training strategies, researchers typically validate ideas through small-scale experiments
and then extrapolate their performance to larger regimes using scaling laws. By
leveraging such reliable extrapolation, it becomes possible to iterate efficiently at
smaller scales while identifying the approaches most likely to perform optimally in
full-scale training. As a result, neural scaling laws have become a standard principle in
the development of state-of-the-art foundation models, including Chinchilla 70B [30],
PaLM 540B [9], GPT-4 [6], and many others [31–39].
Although emergent abilities and neural scaling laws have been empirically vali-
dated across a wide range of foundation models, theoretical understanding of these
2


phenomena remains limited. In this paper, we attempt to propose a rigorous math-
ematical framework to analyze ermergent intelligence and scaling laws. Our central
observation is that intelligence arises as an emergent phenomenon characterized by
a transition from finite knowledge to effectively infinite knowledge. This perspective
naturally motivates the possibility of using limit theory to formalize ermergent intelli-
gence, as fingding irrational numbers through limit of rational numbers. Specifically,
we introduce a three-dimensional function E(N, P, K) to quantify the intelligent behav-
ior (i.e., generalization capability) of foundation models, where N represents the data
size (i.e., the number of data points for training foundation models), P represents
the model size (i.e., the number of model parameters), and K represents the training
steps of optimization algorithms (closely related to the amount of computation). To
understand ermergent intelligence, it is essential to study the asymptotic behavior
of E(N, P, K) in the limit as N →∞, P →∞, and K →∞, corresponding to the
regime of infinite knowledge, architecture and training steps. Under this formulation,
ermergent intelligence can then be rationally characterized by the existence of the limit
limN,P,K→∞E(N, P, K). Furthermore, when this limit exists (denoted by E(∞, ∞, ∞)),
the scaling laws of foundation models can be explicitly revealed by the rate at which
E(N, P, K) converges to E(∞, ∞, ∞).
To characterize foundation models in the infinite-parameter regime, we introduce
an infinite-dimensional system termed the limit architecture, defined as the infinite
composition of stacked basic functional blocks. The properties and behavior of this
limit architecture, as quantified by its generalization performance ε(∞, ∞, ∞), pro-
vide fundamental insights into the mechanisms underlying ermergent intelligence
in foundation models. We introduce the Lip constant, Lip(T), as a key metric to
characterize the existence of the limit architecture, and establish necessary and suf-
ficient conditions under which such a limit exists. Moreover, we propose a standard
error decomposition of ε(N, P, K) −ε(∞, ∞, ∞), which separates the total error
into three components: the optimization (weight) error ε(N, P, K) −ε(N, P, ∞),
the architecture error ε(N, P, ∞) −ε(N, ∞, ∞), and the statistical (sample) error
ε(N, ∞, ∞)−ε(∞, ∞, ∞). We further formalize the conditions under which these error
components arise and establish corresponding upper bounds, which enable us to derive
explicit scaling laws with respect to data size, model size, and training steps.
In summary, our theoretical findings are mainly three-fold:
• Ermergent intelligence. The existence of ermergent intelligence critically depends
on the properties of the basic building blocks. Specifically, let {Ti}, i = 1, 2, · · · ,
denote the sequence of basic blocks in a foundation model. These blocks satisfy the
self-mapping condition, and there exists a constant K such that Lip(Ti) ≤1 for
all i > K. Moreover, the sequence {Ti} converges to a projection operator T, i.e.,
Ti →T, with ∥Ti −T∥∈ℓ1, which corresponds to a condensing property. We show
that these conditions are necessary and sufficient for the existence of ermergent
intelligence, and under the conditions, the limit architecture of foundation models
can be well approximated by a finite composition of stacked basic functional blocks.
• Scaling laws. We employ the standard error decomposition to analyze the discrep-
ancy between E(N, P, K) and E(∞, ∞, ∞), and provide the upper bounds estimation
for the weight error, architecture error and sample error separately. The bounds

illustrate that the scaling laws of training steps and model size follow exponential
law, and scaling law of data size follows a power law.
• Empirical validation. Experimental results demonstrate that the Lip constant
effectively characterizes the properties of basic blocks and serves as a powerful
criterion for evaluating the usability of network architectures, i.e., yielding a stable
architecture. Empirical analysis on state-of-the-art open-source foundation models
further supports the condensing property as a core condition for the existence of
ermergent intelligence.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Related work is reviewed in Section 2.
The formulation of ermergent intelligence and scaling laws from a limit-theoretic
perspective is presented in Section 3. Section 4 introduces the main theoretical tools,
including the standard error decomposition framework, the limit architecture, and
the Lip constant. The necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of the
limit architecture are established in Section 5. Sections 6 and 7 present the existence
conditions for ermergent intelligence and the corresponding scaling laws, respectively.
Experimental validations of the theoretical results are provided in Sections 8 and 9.
Finally, we conclude with a discussion of open problems.
2 Related Work
2.1 Emergence Ability in Foundation Models.
Emergence as an idea has long been discussed in domains such as system science,
physics and biology [25–27], etc. For example, Anderson [25] states that “emergent
abilities for complex systems are those properties that (1) emerge at each level of
complexity and (2) cannot be understood simply by analyzing the single components
‘behavior’ ”. Hopfield [40] studies emergent properties in simple-structured neural
networks with neurons having elementary properties, and states that “computational
properties of use to biological organisms or the construction of computers can emerge as
collective properties of systems having a large number of simple equivalent components
(or neurons)”. For foundation models, Wei et al., [22] adds two important concepts
based on previous definitions, including the unpredictability and the magnitude of
the performance increase, and states that “An ability is emergent if it is not present
in smaller models but is present in larger models. Emergent abilities would not have
been directly predicted by extrapolating a scaling law from small-scale models. When
visualized via a scaling curve, emergent abilities show a clear pattern–performance is
near-random until a certain critical threshold of scale is reached, after which performance
increases to substantially above random”. This definition should be the first LLM-
specific definition and has been mostly most used in the current academic literatures
[24, 41, 42]. Recent work [41] shows that the seemingly sharp and unpredictable
emergence of capabilities is largely driven by the use of nonlinear evaluation metrics,
such as accuracy. In contrast, when performance is assessed using linear metrics (e.g.,
token edit distance), model improvements tend to be smooth and predictable.
Two different approaches have been adopted to analyze ermergent intelligence. In
the complex system science [43], specific dynamic models are used to characterize
4


the behavior of emergence. Scaling is often applied to emergence in complex systems
to demonstrate how “more is different”, and emergent abilities could be understood
through an analogy to phase transitions, e.g., [44–47]. These methods often analyze
emergent property with the temporal variable, while foundation models primarily
focus on variables like model size P, data size D and training steps T, often rendering
them unsuitable for direct application in this context. Besides, the “broken symmetry”
assumption in physics [25], grounded in a specific “material basis”, does not lend itself
directly to modeling the ermergent intelligence of foundation models.
For foundation models, some studies explore to use different tools to help under-
stand emergent abilities, e.g., analyzing loss function and training dynamics [39],
quantization[48], task complexity [49], etc. Besides, emergent abilities are manifested
through specific capabilities, such as in-context learning [50–52], symbolic abstrac-
tion [53], RL-enhanced reasoning [54–56], LLMs-powered agents [57, 58], etc. Existing
approaches to ermergent intelligence have been predominantly empirical, with rela-
tively little work on rigorous mathematical foundations. In this paper, we make an
attempt to develop a preliminary mathematical framework for formalizing ermergent
intelligence from the perspective of limit theory.
2.2 Scaling Law in Foundation Models
Scaling laws have been proposed to analyze the behavior of deep learning across diverse
domains and tasks. Investigations into the relationship between generalization error,
training data size, and model capacity date back to before the era of deep learning
[59]. For deep neural networks, Hestness et al. [60] observes that performance improves
according to a power-law scaling behavior across a variety of domains, including
machine translation, language modeling, image processing, and speech recognition.
Importantly, these scaling relationships are shown to persist across model improvements.
Recently, Kaplan et al. [29] pushes the scale of these studies further into large language
models, studying power laws for models up to 1.5B parameters trained on 23B tokens
to determine the optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget. Subsequent studies
[30] revisit this issue and find that Kaplan scaling law significantly underestimate
the amount of data required for optimal training, although substantial procedural
differences make it difficult to pinpoint the source of this discrepancy. As a result, many
subsequent LLMs [7, 33] have been trained following the Chinchilla scaling laws [30].
Besiroglu et al. [34] revisit the methodology of Hoffmann et al. [30] and report that the
confidence intervals in the original study appear implausibly narrow. In a related line
of research, Porian et al. [61] examine discrepancies between the scaling laws proposed
by Kaplan et al. [29] and those derived under the Chinchilla framework [30].
Since then, researchers have investigated various aspects of scaling in language
models. Hernandez et al. [62] analyze scaling laws governing transfer across distributions
in fine-tuning settings. Aghajanyan et al. [63] explore scaling behaviors in multimodal
foundation models. Poli et al. [64] extend scaling studies to hybrid architectures such as
Mamba [65], demonstrating the effectiveness of this emerging model family. Krajewski
et al. [66] characterize differences in scaling properties between dense transformers and
mixture of expert models. Gadre et al. [67] show that the loss of over-trained models,
trained past compute-optimality, is predictable, and propose a scaling law relating loss
5


to average downstream task performance. [68] revisits scaling laws by examining the
impact of data quality and training strategies on model performance. A key limitation
of existing scaling laws is their disregard for inference costs, which dominate the long-
term expenses of utilizing large models in real-world applications. Sardana et al. [69]
modify the Chinchilla scaling laws to account for both the computational and real-world
costs of inference. The growing adoption of LLMs in reasoning systems also highlights
the need for scaling frameworks that explicitly account for inference costs [55, 70–72].
Recently, some theoretical studies of scaling laws are proposed. The scaling law
for linear models with structured (nonisotropic) covariates, including infinite-width
kernel regression, have been analyzed using tools from statistical physics and random
matrix theory [73–78]. For example, Mei et al. [78] analyze a linear model with random
projections of isotropic covariates. Bahri et al. [76] consider a linear teacher-student
model under a power-law spectrum assumption on the covariates, and they showed that
the test loss of the ordinary least square estimator decreases following a power law in
data size when the model size is infinite. Furthermore, some researches analyze (precise)
generalization error of simple closed-form estimators such as ridge regression [79–82].
While they study the limiting effects of model size and data size, some works also
study the dependence on training steps. Bordelon et al. [83] consider a linear random
feature model and analyze the test loss of the solution found by (batch) gradient
flow. They focused on the bottleneck regimes where two of the data size, model size
and traning steps are infinite, and showed that the risk has a power-law decay in the
remaining quantity. Lin et al. [84] consider a linear predictor trained by one-pass SGD
with geometrically decaying stepsizes, and demonstrate that small variance error is
due to the implicit regularization effect of SGD. High dimensional limits of SGD have
been analyzed with Volterra integral equations in the offline case [85] or with recursive
matrix equations in the online case [86]. Based on this theoretical foundation, [87]
uses phase-plane analysis to characterize scaling laws in the compute-limited, infinite-
data regime. Li et al. [88] establish a functional scaling law that captures the full loss
trajectory under arbitrary learning rate schedules. Besides, existing scaling analyses
for the additive setting [89, 90] explicitly decompose the loss into an independent sum,
simplifying the analysis due to task decoupling. On the other hand, some researches
study the (online) SGD training dynamics and sample complexity of learning a two-
layer neural network, e.g., [91, 92]. However, relatively little theory is known about
how these three factors—model size, data size, and training steps—jointly determine
scaling behavior in deep architectures. In this paper, we aim to address this gap.

4 Research Tools
4.1 Standard Error Decomposition
To study existence of the limit for performance function E(N, P, K), we employ the
following error decomposition framework commonly used in statistical learning theory

10 Conclusion
In this work, we have proposed a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding
ermergent intelligence and scaling law from a limit perspective. We formulate a
foudation model as the composition of stacked basic functional blocks, and introduce
the limit architecture to embody the infinite-parameters limit of the foundation models,
corresponding to an infinite-dimensional system. Our theory reveals that ermergent
intelligence originates from the existence of the limit architecture, and that emergent
abilities correspond precisely to the learning behavior of this limit architecture. We
further introduce the Lip constant of nonlinear operators to precisely quantify properties
of the basic blocks, and prove that existence of the limit architecture is guaranteed
if and only if there exists a constant K > 0 such that Lip(Ti) ≤1, ∀i ≥K, and
the sequence {Ti} satisfies a condensing property by utilizing theory of Lipschitz
dual operator and spectral theory of compact operators. Besides, we derive scaling
laws showing that the performance function of foundation models depends on data
size, model size and training steps, following the scaling βK + Lip(T)P + N
1
2 . Our
theoretical analysis reveals that emergent intelligence is governed by training steps,
data scale, and model architecture, with the properties of basic building blocks playing
a central role. We show that the critical condition Lip(T) = 1 aligns with prior
findings [1, 2], providing theoretical support. Moreover, although emergent intelligence
originates from an infinite-dimensional system, it can be effectively realized via finite-
dimensional architectures, offering a theoretical explanation for empirical observations
[3]. Empirically, we demonstrate that the Lip constant takes a crucial role in evaluating
the usability of foundation models, and could help assess architectural stability. We
further substantiate the condensing property in state-of-the-art open-source foundation
models.
Our analysis assumes that foundation models are constructed by stacking basic
functional blocks. An interesting extension is to consider more general composition
mechanisms, such as residual connections and mixture-of-experts architectures, and
to derive corresponding conditions for the existence of a limit architecture. Another
promising direction is to characterize the precise form of the limit architecture and
leverage its properties to provide theoretical guidance for the architectural design of
foundation models. Finally, our limit theory suggests that foundation models may
achieve benign overfitting by enforcing the existence of a limit architecture. This offers
a novel perspective on mitigating overfitting, contrasting with the traditional statistical
learning paradigm that relies on controlling the complexity of the hypothesis space.

Abstract: Emergent intelligence have played a major role in the modern AI development, manifesting as previously unobserved capabilities enabled by scaling model parame- ters. While existing studies primarily rely on empirical observations to characterize this phenomenon, a rigorous theoretical framework remains underexplored. This study attempts to develop a mathematical approach to formalize emergent intelli- gence from the perspective of limit theory. Specifically, we introduce a performance function E(N, P, K), dependent on data size N, model size P and training steps K, to quantify intelligence behavior. We posit that intelligence emerges as a transition from finite to effectively infinite knowledge, and thus recast emergent intelligence as the existence of the limit limN,P,K→∞E(N, P, K), with emer- gent abilities corresponding to the limiting behavior. Moreover, we show that the scaling laws of foundation models are approximately governed by the convergence rate of E(N, P, K) to its asymptotic value E(∞, ∞, ∞). This limit theory helps reveal that emergent intelligence originates from the existence of a parameter-limit architecture (referred to as the limit architecture), and that emergent intelligence rationally corresponds to the learning behavior of this limit system. By introducing tools from nonlinear Lipschitz operator theory, including charac- teristic constant Lip(T ) of Lipschitz operator, theory of Lipschitz dual operator and spectral theory of compact operators, we prove that the necessary and suf- ficient conditions for existence of the limit architecture is (1) Lip(Ti) ≤1 for all i > K, for some constant K; (2) there exists a projection operator T such that ∥Ti −T ∥= ϵi, where P∞ i=1 ϵi < ∞. Furthermore, we derive the scaling law of foundation models by leveraging tools of Lipschitz operator and covering number. Theoretical results show that: (1) emergent intelligence is governed by ddd1 arXiv:2604.24037v1 [cs.LG] 27 Apr 2026 three key factors-the number of training steps, the size of the training data, and the model architecture, where the properties of basic blocks play a crucial role in constructing foundation models; (2) the critical condition Lip(T ) = 1 for emergent intelligence is consistent with existing findings [1, 2], thereby providing theoretical support for these results; (3) emergent intelligence is determined by an infinite-dimensional system, yet can be effectively realized in practice through a finite-dimensional architecture, offering theoretical justification for the empirical findings in [3]. Our empirical results corroborate these theoretical findings.
